summary: Specifies how IP and ARP packets are carried over Fibre Channel, and how IP addresses are resolved there. It was replaced by RFC 4338.

eli5.summary: A way to make internet messages ride on a fast storage-network cable, plus a method for finding who is who on it.

questions: how does ip run over fibre channel
how are devices addressed on fibre channel
what is the ip mtu on fibre channel
subtitle: How to send internet messages over a high-speed storage network and resolve addresses there.

tldr.problem: Fibre Channel is a gigabit-speed network mostly used for storage (SCSI), but there was no clear standard for how to run IP and ARP over it. The existing FC standard incompletely specified IP encapsulation.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC specifies how to wrap IPv4 and ARP packets inside Fibre Channel frames, define appropriate message sizes (MTU), and describe address resolution. It uses a Fibre Channel Address Resolution Protocol (FARP) to map ethernet MAC addresses to volatile Fibre Channel port IDs.
tldr.outcome: Servers can now communicate with each other over Fibre Channel using IP, useful for clustering and storage-area networking. The specification was replaced by RFC 4338.

facts.label: WW_PN (MAC) width
facts.value: 64 bits (48 bits IEEE MAC plus 16-bit authority)

today: RFC 2625 was a Proposed Standard defining IP and ARP over Fibre Channel. It was obsoleted by RFC 4338, which updated the specification.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Fibre Channel is a high-speed serial interface technology used primarily for Storage Area Networking (SAN). Until now, it was almost exclusively used with the SCSI protocol for storage device communication. Servers still communicate with each other over traditional LANs. This RFC bridges the gap: it specifies how to send IP packets over Fibre Channel, enabling server-to-server communication and clustering over the faster storage network.

The challenge is two-fold. First, IP and ARP packets must be wrapped in Fibre Channel frame format with the correct headers and sizes. Second, address resolution must work: just as ARP maps IP addresses to Ethernet MAC addresses, Fibre Channel requires mapping from MAC addresses to volatile port identifiers, which the RFC calls FARP (Fibre Channel Address Resolution Protocol).
sections.eli5: A storage cable talks a different language than the internet. To send internet messages on it, you need translation: the right wrapping, the right size, and a way for devices to find each other.

sections.title: Encapsulation and Frame Format
sections.content:
Every IP or ARP packet is wrapped inside a Fibre Channel sequence, which is a series of frames. Each frame has a standard FC header (24 bytes) and carries a variable data payload (0 to 2112 bytes). The first frame of an IP sequence includes a Network_Header (16 bytes) that carries the source and destination MAC addresses in a specific format. All IP and ARP payloads use an 8-byte LLC/SNAP header before the actual IP or ARP data, following IEEE 802.2 standards.

The IP MTU is restricted to 65,280 bytes (leaving room for the 16-byte FC Network_Header and 8-byte LLC/SNAP header within the 65,536-byte FC sequence payload limit). ARP packets are always 28 bytes and fit in a single frame. Different Fibre Channel topologies (point-to-point, private loop, public loop, fabric) use different broadcast mechanisms for ARP, but the frame format and encapsulation remain the same.
sections.eli5: Every message is a Russian doll: the IP packet goes inside an 8-byte label, then inside a 16-byte address tag on the first envelope, then into FC frames. Each step has a specific size.

sections.title: ARP and Address Resolution
sections.content:
Address resolution happens in two layers. First, standard ARP resolves an IP address to a Fibre Channel MAC address (the 48-bit World Wide Port Name, or WW_PN). A node sends an ARP Request broadcast; any node with the matching IP address responds with an ARP Reply containing its MAC address. The RFC details how broadcasts work in each Fibre Channel topology: in a private loop, nodes use special signaling; in a public loop or fabric, broadcasts reach all ports through fabric switches.

Second, FARP resolves a MAC address (WW_PN) to a volatile 24-bit Port_ID, which is needed because port IDs change when topology changes. FARP uses Extended Link Services (ELS) commands: a FARP-REQ broadcast asks "who has this MAC address?" and the responding node sends back a FARP-REPLY with its current Port_ID. The RFC also optionally defines Inverse ARP (InARP) to do the reverse: learn an IP address from a known MAC and Port_ID.
sections.eli5: First you ask "What is the address of server Bob?" and someone replies "MAC 00:11:22:33:44:55." Then you ask "Where is MAC 00:11:22:33:44:55 right now?" and someone replies "At port 0x123456." Then you can send.

sections.title: Topologies and Fibre Channel Services
sections.content:
Fibre Channel defines several topologies where IP can run. Point-to-point is the simplest: two nodes directly connected. Private loops connect multiple nodes in a ring; broadcasts are sent with special loop signals. Public loops connect to a fabric switch; the switch propagates broadcasts to all connected devices. Fabric topology uses switches; nodes connect directly to switches and broadcasts are handled by the fabric.

Fibre Channel also defines Classes of Service (1, 2, 3) that determine reliability and flow control. Class 1 provides connection-oriented delivery with guaranteed ordering. Class 2 offers frame delivery without ordering guarantees. Class 3 is connectionless and best-effort. This RFC supports all three classes for IP data, though ARP requests always use Class 3 (best-effort broadcast). The RFC also specifies which FC Extended Link Services (ELS) commands must be supported, including FLOGI (fabric login), PLOGI (port login), and the FARP-specific commands.
sections.eli5: Devices can be wired as a ring, daisy-chain, or star. Some topologies promise the message arrives; others just do their best. The RFC says when to use each kind.

sections.title: Implementation Requirements and Security
sections.content:
All implementations must support at least the maximally minimum IP packet size: a 60-byte IP header plus an 8-byte payload (68 bytes total) wrapped with the 16-byte FC Network_Header and 8-byte LLC/SNAP header, requiring a 92-byte FC data field. This ensures IP fragmentation and reassembly work correctly everywhere.

Security is handled by existing Fibre Channel mechanisms; IP and ARP add no new security risks. The RFC requires that logins between ports (FLOGI for fabric, PLOGI for peer ports) use Fibre Channel versions at least 4.3, ensures proper flow control with credits, and specifies that ARP servers are not supported (broadcast-based ARP is used instead). The specification is designed to work with existing, stable Fibre Channel implementations without requiring new security infrastructure.
sections.eli5: Everyone must be able to handle tiny fragments. The cable's own security is enough; we are not adding locks. Make sure devices shake hands properly when they connect.

fields.name: LLC/SNAP
fields.desc: 8-byte IEEE 802.2 header identifying the protocol as IP.

fields.name: IP Header
fields.desc: 20-byte fixed IP header, up to 40 bytes of options.

fields.name: IP Data
fields.desc: IP payload and optional headers; maximum 65,280 bytes total with header.
